stem: Which additional fact would be enough to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$?
stimulus: A folklore studies archive records two triangular embroidery motifs as triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$. You already know that $AB = DE$ and $BC = EF$.
explanation: You already have two pairs of equal sides. To finish SAS, you need the angles between those sides to be equal. In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ sits between $AB$ and $BC$. In triangle $DEF$, angle $E$ sits between $DE$ and $EF$. So $\angle B = \angle E$ completes SAS. This is the step behind every SAT question that asks which extra fact proves two triangles congruent: first find which angle sits between the sides you were given.

A.why: Angle $A$ is not between $AB$ and $BC$, so this gives you side-side-angle (SSA). SSA is not a congruence criterion, because two different triangles can share two sides and an angle that isn't between them.

C.why: Angle $C$ is not between $AB$ and $BC$ either, so this is SSA again. An equal angle only completes SAS when it sits between the two equal sides.

D.why: This follows directly from the two facts you were given, so it adds nothing new. A fact you can already get from the givens cannot prove anything more.

subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?

stem: Which additional fact would be enough to prove that triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$?
stimulus: A sports science lab models two leg positions as triangles $PQR$ and $STU$. You already know that $\angle P = \angle S$.
explanation: AA similarity needs two pairs of equal angles. You have one pair, $\angle P = \angle S$, and $\angle Q = \angle T$ is the second pair, so the triangles are similar. This is the step behind every SAT question that asks which extra fact proves two triangles similar: count the equal angle pairs you have and look for the one you are missing.

B.why: One pair of equal sides and one pair of equal angles don't meet any similarity criterion. You still need a second angle pair, or sides in proportion around the equal angle.

C.why: These sides meet at angle $Q$ and angle $T$, not at the equal angles $P$ and $S$. Proportional sides prove similarity only when the equal angle sits between them (SAS~). Here the angle isn't between them, which is SSA, so it proves nothing.

D.why: This only gives a size to the angle pair you already have. You still have just one pair of equal angles, and AA needs two.

stem: Which additional fact would be enough to prove that line $m$ is parallel to line $n$?
stimulus: On a city map, two straight streets lie along line $m$ and line $n$. A third straight street, along line $t$, crosses both of them.
choices: A pair of vertical angles at line $m$ are equal.
A pair of alternate interior angles are equal.
A linear pair of angles at line $n$ sum to $180^\circ$.
A pair of same-side interior angles are equal.
explanation: If the alternate interior angles formed by transversal $t$ are equal, then lines $m$ and $n$ are parallel. This is one of the standard tests for parallel lines. This is the step behind every SAT question that asks which angle fact proves two lines parallel: the fact has to compare an angle at one line with an angle at the other line.

A.why: Vertical angles are equal wherever any two lines cross, whether $m$ and $n$ are parallel or not. A fact that is always true can't prove anything.

C.why: A linear pair always sums to $180^\circ$, because the two angles lie on a straight line. It's true for any crossing, and it only involves line $n$, so it tells you nothing about how $n$ relates to $m$.

D.why: You mixed up the rule. Same-side interior angles prove parallel lines when they sum to $180^\circ$, not when they are equal. Equal same-side interior angles would only be enough if both happened to be $90^\circ$.

stem: Which additional fact would be enough to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$?
stimulus: A printmaker carves two triangular shapes into a woodblock. In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $\angle B = 60^\circ$. In triangle $DEF$, $\angle D = 50^\circ$.
explanation: The angles of triangle $ABC$ sum to $180^\circ$, so $\angle C = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 60^\circ = 70^\circ$. If $\angle F = 70^\circ$, the triangles share two pairs of equal angles, $50^\circ$ and $70^\circ$, so they are similar by AA. This is the step behind SAT questions where the matching angle isn't given directly: you use the $180^\circ$ sum to find it.

B.why: You made a slip finding the third angle. $180 - 50 - 60 = 70$, not $80$. With $\angle E = 80^\circ$, triangle $DEF$ has angles of $50^\circ$, $80^\circ$, and $50^\circ$, which don't match triangle $ABC$.

C.why: One pair of equal sides and one pair of equal angles don't meet any similarity criterion. You still need a second pair of equal angles.

D.why: These sides meet at angle $E$ and angle $B$, not at the known equal angles $D$ and $A$. Proportional sides need the equal angle between them (SAS~). This is SSA, so it proves nothing.
